summary: Astrid is called after the louder applicants and immediately establishes that she will answer for herself rather than through Carrie.

panelPlan.action: Astrid moves to the individual questioning position without special framing.
The Hearing Officer checks whether Astrid wants caseworker assistance.
Carrie turns slightly toward Astrid but does not speak.
Astrid answers directly.
Carrie sits back. The Hearing Officer continues without treating the answer as remarkable.

dialogueInline.text: Do you want Ms. Carrie to help answer if you have trouble with a question?
If I need her, I ask.

directionInline.text: Underplay Astrid's turn. No hero framing, applause, or sudden transformation.

summary: One compact line of questioning reveals Astrid's practical independence: she can get home, buy what the household needs, and has neighborhood relationships Carrie did not catalogue as hers.
settingText: Hearing chamber with two restrained reader-facing ordinary-life cutaways.

panelPlan.action: The officer asks one practical question tied to the independent-adult classification.
Astrid answers in concrete landmarks rather than transit jargon.
Astrid alone steps off a bus near the familiar blue-doored church carrying groceries; she moves with practiced certainty.

panelPlan.shotType: medium on Hearing Officer and Astrid
panelPlan.action: The officer follows with ordinary household and neighborhood questions.
Astrid at the bodega counter exchanges a familiar nod with the owner while choosing soap and needles; the Upstairs Neighbor passes her in the building hall in a separate sliver of the panel.
Carrie looks at her generic neighborhood-contact notes. Gunnar realizes Astrid knows routes he never taught her.

dialogueInline.text: If you left this building alone, could you get home and get what the household needs on the way?
Yes. Train if it runs. Bus to the blue church if it does not. Food, soap, needles. I know the stores.
Who would know you there?
Store owner. Woman upstairs. Woman with red cart.
I did not teach her that way.
And I wrote those down as household contacts.

directionInline.text: The two cutaways are reader-facing illustrations of ordinary accumulated life, not evidence projected in the hearing. Keep the reveal mundane.

summary: Astrid completes the proof without a montage: she can ask for clarification, manages an ordinary day by choice, and makes clear that mutual reliance inside the household is not legal dependency on Bjorn or Carrie.

panelPlan.action: The officer asks a bureaucratically phrased independence question.
Astrid refuses the wording rather than the question.
The officer simplifies without irritation.
Astrid answers with the ordinary shape of her day and no effort to impress the room.
The officer asks the question that matters to the old household classification.
Bjorn hears Astrid define the relationship without insult; Carrie does not translate or soften it.

dialogueInline.text: Do you independently procure ordinary necessities and manage routine travel without household supervision?
I know those words. Not why you put them together.
Do you run your own day?
Yes. I shop. I wash clothes. I go where I need. Sometimes where I want.
Do you need Bjorn to make those decisions?
No.
He needs me sometimes. I need him sometimes. That is different.

summary: After Astrid's testimony, the Hearing Officer returns to the unresolved record defect: strong individual lives do not automatically erase an old legal classification.
settingText: Same hearing chamber, after Astrid returns to the applicant table.

panelPlan.action: Astrid returns to the applicant table. The Hearing Officer stacks the testimony notes beside the old master household record.
The officer acknowledges what the testimony has established.
The old field HOUSEHOLD RESPONSIBLE ADULT — BJORN remains visible on the intake record.
Carrie understands the distinction between facts and the legal record.
The officer states the remaining finding she needs.

dialogueInline.text: I have heard five adults describe separate lives and separate intentions.
I still have a record that says one of you is responsible for the other four.
Because I put it there.
Then I need to know whether it was only an intake shortcut, or whether it still describes this household.

summary: Carrie owns the original classification instead of defending her file, explaining why it was reasonable during emergency intake and why leaving it unchanged became inaccurate.

panelPlan.action: Carrie keeps the old intake sheet open in front of her.
The officer asks whether the designation was factually true at intake.
Carrie answers without blaming the software or pretending the choice was meaningless.
She then states the part that costs her professionally.
The applicants hear Carrie acknowledge that the case record lagged behind their lives.

dialogueInline.text: At intake, the system required one responsible adult. Bjorn could communicate enough to get five people housed. I chose him.
Was that false?
No. That day, it was useful and mostly true.
I should have amended it when it stopped being true.
All right. Then we test whether it stopped.

summary: The Hearing Officer tests the old hierarchy directly by asking whether Bjorn can consent, decide, or speak for the other adults; each answer separates respect for Bjorn from legal dependence on him.

panelPlan.action: The officer addresses the four adults listed under Bjorn's old responsible-adult designation.
First Male Kin answers first, matter-of-fact.
Gunnar answers with the distinction he has learned to live by.
Second Male Kin answers without looking to Bjorn.
Astrid answers last and shortest.
Bjorn listens to four refusals of legal dependence without treating any as disloyalty.

dialogueInline.text: Can Bjorn consent to permanent status, housing decisions, or future residence on your behalf?
He can tell me what he thinks.
He can advise me.
He cannot choose where I stay.
No.
